item.description: arXiv:2610.18528v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We characterize several properties of higher-arity function classes, specifically finite $\VC_k$-dimension, slicewise finite $\VC$-dimension, and finite slicewise Littlestone dimension, in terms of generalizations of Rademacher complexity. These characterizations sets up simple new proofs of several results on finite $\VC_k$-dimension and slicewise finite $\VC$-dimension. These include the preservation of finite $\VC_k$-dimension under taking expectations and uniform law of large numbers statements for both properties. All of these results apply naturally to real-valued function classes as well as boolean-valued classes. We also prove a new adversarial uniform law of large numbers for classes with finite slicewise Littlestone dimension.
item.dc:creator: Aaron Anderson, Henry Towsner

item.title: Optimal Support Size Testing
item.description: arXiv:2610.18723v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present an optimal tester for support size that determines whether an unknown probability distribution is supported on $n$ elements or $\varepsilon$-far away (in total variation distance) with sample complexity $\Theta(\frac{n}{\varepsilon\log(n)})$, improving the prior best $O(\frac{n}{\varepsilon\log(n)} \log(\min\{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}, n\}))$ due to Ferreira Pinto Jr. and Harms (STOC 2025). As a generalization, we provide a pretty good lower bound on support size.
item.dc:creator: Qisheng Wang

item.title: Compatibility-based Bayesian inference: asymptotic limits, variational principles, and Wasserstein geometry
item.description: arXiv:2105.01962v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) replaces intractable likelihood evaluations with comparisons between observed and simulated data. We develop a measure-theoretic formulation of discrepancy-based Bayesian inference in which compatibility is encoded through nonnegative weights. For vanishing thresholds, we establish convergence of the corresponding posterior distributions in total variation. In the large-sample regime, we identify conditions under which the posterior converges to the prior conditioned on an asymptotic compatibility region, showing that concentration need not occur at a fixed positive tolerance. We also derive persistence bounds under weaker assumptions and prove stability of the associated entropy-regularized variational problems. For Wasserstein discrepancies, we obtain a geometric representation through distances from compatibility balls and an exact variational reduction to probability distributions over model laws.
item.dc:creator: Marco Tarsia, Antonietta Mira, Daniele Cassani

item.title: Concentration inequalities for leave-one-out cross validation
item.description: arXiv:2211.02478v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this article we prove that estimator stability, together with a gradient-growth condition on the expected fitted loss, is enough to provide concentration bounds for leave-one-out cross-validation in a general framework. In particular, we provide concentration bounds beyond Lipschitz continuity assumptions on the loss or on the estimator. We obtain our results by relying on random variables with distribution satisfying the logarithmic Sobolev inequality, providing us a relatively rich class of distributions. We illustrate our method by considering several interesting examples, including linear regression, kernel density estimation, and stabilized/truncated estimators such as stabilized kernel regression.
item.dc:creator: Benny Avelin, Lauri Viitasaari

item.title: Consistency of heritability estimation from summary statistics in high-dimensional linear models
item.description: arXiv:2502.11144v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS), heritability is defined as the fraction of variance of an outcome explained by a large number of genetic predictors in a high-dimensional polygenic linear model. This work studies the asymptotic properties of the most common estimator of heritability from summary statistics called linkage disequilibrium score (LDSC) regression, together with a simpler and closely related estimator called GWAS heritability (GWASH). These estimators are analyzed in their basic versions and under various modifications used in practice including weighting and standardization. We show that, with some variations, two conditions which we call weak dependence (WD) and bounded-kurtosis effects (BKE) are sufficient for consistency of both the basic LDSC with fixed intercept and GWASH estimators, for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian predictors. For Gaussian predictors it is shown that these conditions are also necessary for consistency of GWASH (with truncation) and simulations suggest that necessity holds too when the predictors are non-Gaussian. We also show that, with properly truncated weights, weighting does not change the consistency results, but standardization of the predictors and outcome, as done in practice, introduces bias in both LDSC and GWASH if the two essential conditions are violated. Finally, we show that, when population stratification is present, all the estimators considered are biased, and the bias is not remedied by using the LDSC regression estimator with free intercept, as originally suggested by the authors of that estimator. These findings allow the user of the above estimates to evaluate whether they are useful for the data at hand.
item.dc:creator: David Azriel, Samuel Davenport, Armin Schwartzman

item.title: A unified spectral analysis of high-dimensional linear regression: debiasing and thresholding
item.description: arXiv:2502.17261v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We use spectral analysis to establish a unified theory of debiasing, thresholding, and simultaneous inference for high-dimensional linear regression with ill-conditioned designs. The methods include Ridge regression, spectral cut-off, and iterative and dynamical regression procedures. A common debiasing procedure uses two applications of the original linear algorithm with fixed parameters. Spectral analysis shows that debiasing squares the residual, while implementations based on matrix-vector products require no explicit spectral decomposition. Under explicit design, signal, and moment conditions, we establish maximum-norm consistency, recovery of the population threshold set, and error bounds for coefficient and noise-variance estimation. We derive Gaussian approximations for maximum coordinate errors and, under full column rank and deterministic sequences of regression parameters and thresholds, prove bootstrap validity for simultaneous confidence regions. Under additional regularity and gain conditions, we relate noise-free bias rates to best-worst-case error rates. Sparse and non-sparse regression experiments examine the effects of debiasing and thresholding under specified tuning rules. An elliptic inverse source problem extends the numerical assessment to reconstruction and empirical simultaneous coverage.
item.dc:creator: Ying-Ao Wang, Yunyi Zhang, Ye Zhang

item.title: Stein's unbiased risk estimate and Hyv\"arinen's score matching
item.description: arXiv:2502.20123v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Given a collection of observed signals corrupted with Gaussian noise, how can we learn to optimally denoise them? This fundamental problem arises in both empirical Bayes and generative modeling. In empirical Bayes, the predominant approach is via nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation (NPMLE), while in generative modeling, score matching (SM) methods have proven very successful. In our setting, Hyv\"arinen's implicit SM is equivalent to another classical idea from statistics---Stein's Unbiased Risk Estimate (SURE). Revisiting SURE minimization, we establish, for the first time, that SURE achieves nearly parametric rates of convergence of the regret in the classical empirical Bayes setting with homoscedastic noise. We also prove that SURE-training can achieve fast rates of convergence to the oracle denoiser in a commonly studied misspecified model. We show how to practically implement our method in settings involving heteroscedasticity and side-information, such as in an application to the estimation of economic mobility in the Opportunity Atlas. Our empirical results demonstrate the superior performance of SURE-training over NPMLE under misspecification. Collectively, our findings advance SURE/SM as a strong alternative to the NPMLE for empirical Bayes problems in both theory and practice.
item.dc:creator: Sulagna Ghosh, Nikolaos Ignatiadis, Frederic Koehler, Amber Lee

item.title: From Graphical Lasso to Atomic Norms: High-Dimensional Pattern Recovery
item.description: arXiv:2506.13353v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study high-dimensional precision-matrix estimation with polyhedral atomic-norm penalties on the off-diagonal entries. This framework covers the graphical lasso, $\ell_\infty$-type penalties, SLOPE/OWL penalties, and penalties motivated by colored graphical models. We define the target pattern through the subdifferential face of the dual ball and derive sufficient conditions for exact pattern recovery from the sample covariance matrix. Our analysis introduces two geometric thresholds, a generalized irrepresentability condition, and extends the primal-dual witness method beyond the $\ell_1$ setting. For the graphical lasso, our results yield weaker covariance-deviation requirements and a less restrictive irrepresentability condition than existing theory, leading to sharper asymptotic guarantees. Numerical experiments for several graph topologies show that the resulting bounds are often close to the empirical recovery threshold.
item.dc:creator: Piotr Graczyk, Bartosz Ko{\l}odziejek, Hideto Nakashima, Maciej Wilczy\'nski

item.title: Learning Smooth Populations of Parameters with Trial Heterogeneity
item.description: arXiv:2507.23140v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the classical problem of estimating the mixing distribution of binomial mixtures, but under trial heterogeneity and smoothness. This problem has been studied extensively when the trial parameter is homogeneous, but not under the more general scenario of heterogeneous trials, and only within a low smoothness regime, where the resulting rates are slow. Under the assumption that the density is s-smooth, we derive fast error rates for the kernel density estimator under trial heterogeneity that depend on the harmonic mean of the trials. Importantly, even when reduced to the homogeneous case, our result improves on the state-of-the-art rate of Ye and Bickel (2021). We also study nonparametric estimation of the difference between two densities, which can be smoother than the individual densities, in both i.i.d. and binomial-mixture settings. Our work is motivated by an application in criminal justice: comparing conviction rates of indigent representation in Pennsylvania. We find that the estimated conviction rates for appointed counsel (court-appointed private attorneys) are generally higher than those for public defenders, potentially due to a confounding factor: appointed counsel are more likely to take on severe cases.
item.dc:creator: JungHo Lee, Valerio Ba\'cak, Edward H. Kennedy

item.title: Autoregressive Processes on Stiefel and Grassmann Manifolds
item.description: arXiv:2509.24767v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: System identification methods for autoregressive processes on Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds are presented and studied. We model the system parameters as elements of the orthogonal group and we show that the system can be estimated by averaging over observations. Lastly, we propose an algorithm for computing these system parameters using a conjugate gradient method adapted to Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds.
item.dc:creator: Jordi-Llu\'is Figueras, Aron Persson

item.title: Sparse estimation for the drift of high-dimensional Ornstein--Uhlenbeck processes with i.i.d. paths
item.description: arXiv:2510.21505v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study sparsity-regularized maximum likelihood estimation for the drift parameter of high-dimensional non-stationary Ornstein--Uhlenbeck processes given repeated measurements of i.i.d. paths. In particular, we show that Lasso and Slope estimators can achieve the minimax optimal rate of convergence. We exhibit numerical experiments for sparse estimation methods and show their performance.
item.dc:creator: Shogo Nakakita

item.title: Cluster size distributions of discrete random fields
item.description: arXiv:2601.14586v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study size distributions of finite excursion clusters of discrete random fields on the integer lattice $\mathbb Z^d$. For stationary fields, we assign a unique root to each finite cluster and derive an exact representation of the root Palm size law through joint exceedance and exterior nonexceedance probabilities for complete connected shapes. Root sampling gives each finite cluster equal weight and remains well defined even when infinite components are present. We also study the cluster size law conditional on a specified site being a local maximum above the threshold $u$, providing a local formulation for nonstationary fields. Under stationarity and almost sure cluster finiteness, an exact change of measure shows that peak sampling reweights the root law by the number of local maxima in each cluster. For stationary Gaussian fields satisfying suitable conditions, the total variation distance between these laws decreases exponentially in $u^2$. Guarded spatial Monte Carlo yields unbiased estimators of cluster intensities, estimates of sampling uncertainty from independent realizations, and a finite sample certificate for root truncation error. We further establish sufficient exponential cluster size tail bounds at a fixed threshold and exact logarithmic Gaussian decay rates at a fixed cluster size as $u\to \infty$. The latter rates are characterized by quadratic programs retaining the exterior constraints needed to identify complete components. Numerical illustrations compare direct probability evaluations with Monte Carlo estimates and assess sampling uncertainty and truncation error. The general representations and estimators apply to both Gaussian and non-Gaussian fields, providing a probabilistic foundation for quantifying spatial extent in discretely sampled data.
item.dc:creator: Dan Cheng, John Ginos

item.title: An Operator-Theoretic Analysis of Nonlinear Filtering under Model Misspecification
item.description: arXiv:2607.11378v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study nonlinear filtering with misspecified initial distributions and dynamics, but a correctly specified observation model. Observations are treated as a random process generated by the true model, rather than as fixed realizations, and both the correct filter and the misspecified filter are analyzed under this common observation law. Our main result is a Bayesian total variation balance identity for the expected change in total variation distance under a Bayesian update: a covariance term minus a non-negative remainder. The identity characterizes conditional and averaged update non-expansivity. Combined with prediction contraction, it yields finite-time bounds separating the initialization error from accumulated dynamical discrepancies, while allowing expansive updates. When the averaged updates are non-expansive and a uniform joint prediction--update coefficient is less than one, a persistent dynamical misspecification yields an asymptotic error bound proportional to the one-step discrepancy. When the conditional updates are non-expansive, we characterize an accumulated joint contraction that implies almost-sure and \(L^1\) coalescence of the true and misspecified filters. Finally, we verify update non-expansivity for scalar Gaussian predictive laws under a variance-ordering condition and, separately, derive explicit prediction contraction bounds for truncated kernels and bounded transition functions with elliptically symmetric noise.
item.dc:creator: Fabi\'an Gonz\'alez, \"Omer Deniz Akyildiz, Dan Crisan, Joaqu\'in M\'iguez

item.title: Recovery of latent inner products from an anisotropic Gaussian random geometric graph
item.description: arXiv:2607.23723v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the problem of recovering latent inner products from a random geometric graph with anisotropic Gaussian latent points. More precisely, for an i.i.d. sample $x_1, \dots, x_n \sim N(0,\Sigma)$ where $\Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$, an edge $(i,j)$ is present in the graph if and only if $\langle x_i, x_j \rangle \ge \zeta$ for a threshold $\zeta$. We assume the threshold $\zeta$ to be chosen such that the average edge density of the graph is of constant order. To address the undesired degree fluctuations amplified by the anisotropy of the latent points, we consider the doubly centered adjacency matrix of the graph, and estimate the latent inner products using a rank-$d$ spectral approximation of the doubly centered matrix. The estimator obtains a mean squared error with a rate involving the stable rank of the covariance matrix $\Sigma$. Notably, the rate of estimation matches the state of the art for the isotropic case $\Sigma = I_d$, and permits an ill-conditioned covariance matrix with a diverging condition number. The analysis of the spectral method proceeds via the entrywise Hermite expansion of the doubly centered adjacency matrix with respect to the latent inner products. Instead of the standard trace method, it uses a decoupling argument recently introduced by Kaushik, Romberg, and Muthukumar (2025) to control nonlinear error terms.
item.dc:creator: Cheng Mao, Vidya Muthukumar

item.title: Spectral Dependence of Convex Regularization: Fundamental Limits under Right-Rotationally Invariant Designs
item.description: arXiv:2608.07432v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the fundamental limits of convex-regularized estimation in high-dimensional linear regression with right-rotationally invariant design matrices. We show that the asymptotic risks of convex-penalized least squares estimators are lower bounded by the risk of an approximate message passing algorithm known as Bayes VAMP, and we further characterize when the lower bound is attainable. As a technical ingredient in the proof of our lower bound theorem, we characterize the asymptotic performance of the $\ell_2$-perturbed convex estimator for every fixed perturbation strength $\lambda>0$. This closes a gap in the literature, in which $\lambda$ was required to be sufficiently large or restrictions were imposed on the class of convex estimators. The benefit of our approach is that we can conduct a direct analysis of the spectrum's impact on the lower bound in the high-dimensional limit. In particular, we can show that the lower bound is monotone in an ordering on the limiting spectral distributions of the design matrix. These results isolate how the full singular-value distribution of the design---not merely the aspect ratio or average measurement strength---governs the limitations of convex regularization.
item.dc:creator: Baichen Tan, Audrey Yang, Cynthia Rush

item.title: Covariance and Principal Component Analysis on Riemannian Manifolds and Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2609.15753v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop notions of covariance and principal component analysis (PCA) for probability measures on Riemannian manifolds of bounded geometry and a discrete counterpart for distributions on the vertex sets of weighted simple graphs. Rather than anchoring variation at the Fr\'{e}chet mean, whose uniqueness and usefulness can fail in this context, we consider variation about every point. This leads to a representation of each point on the manifold by a vector field derived from the heat kernel and thus to a map of the underlying manifold into a Hilbert space of vector fields, in which covariance and PCA carry over from the Euclidean setting. A distinguishing feature of this formulation is that one typically obtains infinitely many principal components, capable of capturing highly nonlinear geometric features and patterns of variation. We prove an embedding theorem for the mapping into the space of vector fields and develop two computational reductions of the theory: RiePCA, a finite-dimensional reduction based on vector fields supported on finitely many points, and GraphPCA, a discrete formulation for measures on weighted graphs in which vector fields assign orientations and magnitudes to edges. Numerical examples and experiments illustrate the behavior of the proposed methods on both synthetic and real data.
item.dc:creator: Luiz Hartmann, Wenwen Li, Washington Mio

item.title: Optimal estimation and goodness-of-fit testing of the mean for sparse longitudinal functional data
item.description: arXiv:2609.19889v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the mean function of longitudinal functional data, where each subject contributes a small number of complete profiles over a general domain, observed at random visit times. The mean is projected onto an orthonormal basis in the time direction, and each coefficient function is estimated by a weighted average of the profiles. We consider deterministic and random weights, including closed-form, data-driven weights that dispense with the design density entirely. For each weighting scheme we derive non-asymptotic bounds on the integrated quadratic risk and an explicit optimal truncation level. All schemes share the same convergence rate, which we show to be minimax optimal over the corresponding coefficient-decay class, only the leading constants differ. We also provide a goodness-of-fit test for the mean function, and derive non-asymptotic bounds for the Gaussian approximation of its distribution under both the null and alternative hypotheses. Our estimation and testing procedures are easy to implement, fast, and perform well in applications.
item.dc:creator: Valentin Patilea, Mahdi Saidi

item.title: Rank-one variance inflation in polynomial estimation of signal parameters with a sign-preserving fractional-power basis
item.description: arXiv:2610.05511v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The polynomial maximization method estimates signal parameters in non-Gaussian noise from a finite description of the noise by its moments and cumulants, without a density. Known accuracy results assume that these noise characteristics are known, or use a design in which estimating them jointly costs no accuracy. In practice they are estimated from the residuals of a preliminary fit, and the effect of this substitution on accuracy is unknown. We treat the feasible scheme as a two-step estimator and, for a general smooth signal model in a fixed design, find the increment of its asymptotic covariance in closed form: $\Sigma_{\rm fe}-\Sigma_{\rm or}=c_2(1-g_{\rm or}) Q^{-1}\bar{d}\bar{d}^{\top}Q^{-1}$, a positive semidefinite matrix of rank at most one. Here $c_2$ is the noise variance, $g_{\rm or}\le 1$ the oracle variance reduction factor, and $Q$ and $\bar{d}$ the second-moment matrix and mean of the signal gradient over the design. Estimating the fractional moments that form the weights costs no first-order accuracy, because that block is orthogonal; the whole increment comes from estimating the sign-preserving centering means. The increment lies along the single direction $Q^{-1}\bar{d}$, so linear combinations of the parameters orthogonal to it keep oracle accuracy. In the trace metric the variance reduction factor becomes $g_{\rm fe}=g_{\rm or}+(1-g_{\rm or})R_D$, where $R_D=\|Q^{-1}\bar{d}\|^2/{\rm tr} Q^{-1}$ depends on the design alone. We give four sufficient conditions for first-order oracle equivalence; noise symmetry is not among them. Monte Carlo experiments with a harmonic signal confirm the direction and size of the increment. A covariance estimate that ignores the increment undercovers where non-Gaussianity gives the largest gain, symmetric noise included.
item.dc:creator: Serhii Zabolotnii

item.title: Targeted Data Fusion for Region-Specific Survival Effects in the AMP HIV Prevention Trials
item.description: arXiv:2501.18798v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The Antibody Mediated Prevention (AMP) trials opened a new scientific frontier by showing that passively administered monoclonal broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) could prevent HIV-1 acquisition. The trials enrolled 4,611 participants across four epidemiologically distinct regions, with 174 HIV-1 diagnoses observed during follow-up. Regional heterogeneity in treatment efficacy, together with privacy and regulatory limits on central data pooling, calls for methods that borrow strength across regions without sharing individual-level data. To estimate region- and treatment-specific survival curves under distributional heterogeneity, we develop a federated learning approach that combines site-specific estimators via an L1-regularized criterion that downweights data sources not aligned with the target. We further extend the framework to a general class of causal contrasts, including the survival difference, survival ratio, and restricted mean survival time difference. In the AMP analysis, for example, the standard error of the day-148 survival difference decreased from 0.007 using the target-only estimator to 0.004 using the federated estimator. For women in South Africa, the region-specific analyses provided no strong evidence of an overall VRC01 benefit, consistent with the primary AMP findings. Overall, the proposed approach provides region-adaptive inference with improved precision without sharing individual-level data, while preserving estimation of region-specific treatment effects under cross-region heterogeneity.
item.dc:creator: Yi Liu, Alexander W. Levis, Ke Zhu, Shu Yang, Peter B. Gilbert, Larry Han

item.title: Markovian Continuity of the MMSE
item.description: arXiv:2504.14659v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Minimum mean square error (MMSE) estimation is widely used in signal processing, information theory, and related fields. Despite its practical robustness, the MMSE can be discontinuous under standard notions of stochastic convergence. To bridge this gap, we review classical counterexamples to the continuity of the MMSE and identify two obstructions: failure of second-moment convergence and approximating observations carrying more information about the limit estimand than the limit observation does. Motivated by practical acquisition mechanisms, we study MMSE continuity under two natural constraints: (1) continuity of the second moment, and (2) a degradedness (Markov) restriction ensuring that each approximating observation is no more informative than the limit observation is about the limit estimand. Under these conditions, we establish continuity of the MMSE and of the MMSE estimator. We provide complementary semicontinuity results and continuity guarantees in related settings and establish continuity under linear estimation. We further extend the analysis to the families of Bregman divergences and continuous metric and generalized metric cost functions, including the Kullback-Leibler and Jensen-Shannon divergences as special cases.
item.dc:creator: Elad Domanovitz, Anatoly Khina

item.title: Equilibrium Distribution for t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding with Generalized Kernels
item.description: arXiv:2505.24311v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We extend the results by Auffinger and Fletcher in 2023 on the large-sample limit of t-SNE to a broader class of input and output kernels. We prove that under natural assumptions on the input distribution and the decay of the output kernel, if perplexity scales linearly with data size, the empirical measures and values of minimizers converge to an equilibrium distribution. We conclude with numerical examples comparing different kernels.
item.dc:creator: Yi Gu, Antonio Auffinger

item.title: On the Upper Bounds for the Matrix Spectral Norm
item.description: arXiv:2506.15660v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider the problem of estimating the spectral norm of a matrix using only matrix-vector products. We propose a new Counterbalance estimator that provides upper bounds on the norm and derive probabilistic guarantees on its underestimation. Compared to standard approaches such as the power method, the proposed estimator produces significantly tighter upper bounds in both synthetic and real-world settings. Our method is especially effective for matrices with fast-decaying spectra, such as those arising in deep learning and inverse problems.
item.dc:creator: Alexey Naumov, Maxim Rakhuba, Denis Ryapolov, Sergey Samsonov

item.title: High-Order Error Bounds for Markovian LSA with Richardson-Romberg Extrapolation
item.description: arXiv:2508.05570v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we study the bias and high-order error bounds of the Linear Stochastic Approximation (LSA) algorithm with Polyak-Ruppert (PR) averaging under Markovian noise. We focus on the version of the algorithm with constant step size $\alpha$ and propose a novel decomposition of the bias via a linearization technique. We analyze the structure of the bias and show that the leading-order term is linear in $\alpha$ and cannot be eliminated by PR averaging. To address this, we apply the Richardson-Romberg (RR) extrapolation procedure, which effectively cancels the leading bias term. We derive high-order moment bounds for the RR iterates and show that the leading error term aligns with the asymptotically optimal covariance matrix of the vanilla averaged LSA iterates.
item.dc:creator: Ilya Levin, Alexey Naumov, Sergey Samsonov

item.title: Complexity Dependent Error Rates for Physics-informed Statistical Learning via the Small-ball Method
item.description: arXiv:2510.23149v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Physics-informed statistical learning (PISL) integrates empirical data with physical knowledge to enhance the statistical performance of estimators. While PISL methods are widely used in practice, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of how informed regularization affects statistical properties is still missing. Specifically, two fundamental questions have yet to be fully addressed: (A) what is the trade-off between soft penalties and hard constraints, and (B) what is the statistical gain of incorporating physical knowledge compared to purely data-driven empirical error minimisation. In this paper, we address these questions for PISL in classes of functions whose convex hull satisfies a small-ball condition, in particular convex classes, under physical knowledge expressed as linear equations by developing appropriate complexity dependent error rates based on the small-ball method. We specialise them to linear classes of finite dimension $q$ in which the space of solutions of the equation has dimension $k < q$, and show that (A) the physics-informed estimator attains the error bound of the hard-constrained empirical error minimiser whenever the penalty parameter is above an explicit threshold, and that (B) the penalty improves the error rate from $\sqrt{q/n}$ to $\sqrt{k/n}$ under a second moment condition on the noise only, having the effect of a dimensionality reduction. We also quantify how these conclusions degrade when the equation is misspecified, in terms of the excess residual of the target function. This work establishes a theoretical framework for evaluating the statistical properties of physics-informed estimators in such classes, contributing to closing the gap between statistical theory and practical PISL.
item.dc:creator: Diego Marcondes

item.title: Sampling from multimodal distributions with warm starts: Non-asymptotic bounds for the Reweighted Annealed Leap-Point Sampler
item.description: arXiv:2512.17977v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sampling from multimodal distributions is a central challenge in Bayesian inference and machine learning. In light of hardness results for sampling -- classical MCMC methods, even with tempering, can suffer from exponential mixing times -- a natural question is how to leverage additional information, such as a warm start point for each mode, to enable faster mixing across modes. To address this, we introduce Reweighted ALPS (Re-ALPS), a modified version of the Annealed Leap-Point Sampler (ALPS) that dispenses with the Gaussian approximation assumption. We prove the first polynomial-time bound that works in a general setting, under a natural assumption that each component contains significant mass relative to the others when tilted towards the corresponding warm start point. Similarly to ALPS, we define distributions tilted towards a mixture centered at the warm start points, and at the coldest level, use teleportation between warm start points to enable efficient mixing across modes. In contrast to ALPS, our method does not require Hessian information at the modes, but instead estimates component partition functions via Monte Carlo. This additional estimation step is crucial in allowing the algorithm to handle target distributions with more complex geometries besides approximate Gaussian. For the proof, we show convergence results for Markov processes when only part of the stationary distribution is well-mixing and estimation for partition functions for individual components of a mixture.
item.dc:creator: Holden Lee, Matheau Santana-Gijzen

item.title: Coherent Information Deletion: Bayesian, Generalized Bayesian and Possibilistic Unlearning
item.description: arXiv:2602.09061v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Bayes' theorem admits an information processing interpretation due to Zellner (1988): under the Shannon information criterion, the posterior is the unique rule that processes prior and data information without information loss. We revisit these ideas from the perspective of information deletion. Given a posterior based on a complete dataset, what distribution should replace it when a subset of the data is removed? For ordinary Bayesian inference, we show that the corresponding information deletion objective is uniquely minimized by the leave-data-out posterior. We then extend the framework beyond likelihood-based inference from Bayes to the generalized Bayesian updating of Bissiri et al.(2016} based on loss functions. Requiring deletion to be coherent under sequential removal of loss contributions yields a deletion rule that exactly recovers the generalized posterior based only on the retained information. We further develop an axiomatic theory, beyond probabilistic inference, for possibilistic deletion and show that the same information-deletion perspective leads to a principled rule for exact possibilistic unlearning. Finally, restricting these exact deletion principles to tractable families leads naturally to variational Bayesian, generalized Bayesian, and maxitive possibilistic unlearning.
item.dc:creator: Hans Montcho, H{\aa}vard Rue, Maurizio Filippone

item.title: Design-based theory for covariate adjustment in generalized pairwise comparisons
item.description: arXiv:2602.18383v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Generalized pairwise comparisons summarize treatment effects in randomized experiments with ordinal, multivariate, or prioritized outcomes. We study optimal covariate adjustment under complete randomization, with potential outcomes and covariates fixed and treatment assignment as the sole source of randomness. We derive the exact randomization variance of the unadjusted estimator and characterize linear calibration adjustments using the between-arm difference in covariate means. The asymptotic variance is a strictly convex quadratic in the adjustment coefficient, yielding a closed-form optimum. The resulting estimator is asymptotically no less efficient than the unadjusted estimator, with an explicit precision gain that clarifies which covariates improve precision. However, natural pair-level and single-arm least squares adjustments generally use weights that differ from the allocation-dependent optimum and can substantially reduce efficiency. We also propose a within-arm variance estimator for asymptotically conservative inference, whose conservatism arises from unidentifiable joint variation in a unit's two potential scores, and show that residualizing each arm on its own projection coefficient saves the discrepancy that governs the efficiency loss of conventional adjustments. In the special case where the comparison function is the outcome difference, our proposed covariate-adjusted estimator is first-order equivalent to the fully interacted regression adjustment of Lin (Ann. Appl. Stat., 2013, 7, 295-318).
item.dc:creator: Xinyuan Chen, Fan Li

item.title: Maximum score and non-smooth M-estimators with multiway dependence
item.description: arXiv:2604.10232v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Under i.i.d. sampling, the maximum score estimator of Manski (1975) converges at the cube-root rate to a non-Gaussian limit. We show that, under multiway dependence and low-level conditions, it is asymptotically normal at a parametric rate in the smallest number of clusters and, when the cluster-level variance is non-degenerate, as fast as regular estimators such as probit. The result rests on a general theory for non-smooth M-estimators, under which a modified bootstrap is first-order valid given a consistent Hessian estimate. With two-way clustering, a cube-root term can remain; under high-level conditions, symmetric bootstrap intervals for suitable scalar parameters still control size uniformly.
item.dc:creator: Harold D. Chiang, Ahnaf Rafi

item.title: Cover meets Robbins while Betting on Bounded Data: $\ln n$ Regret and Almost Sure $\ln\ln n$ Regret
item.description: arXiv:2604.20172v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Consider betting against a sequence of $[0,1]$-valued observations using bets that are fair if the data have a conditional mean $m_0 \in (0,1)$. Cover's universal portfolio algorithm achieves a worst-case regret of $O(\ln n)$ compared to the best constant bet in hindsight, and this logarithmic order is unimprovable against adversarial data. We construct an explicit full-support Robbins mixture that combines insights from Robbins and Cover. It retains $O(\ln n)$ regret on every path while also eventually satisfying $R_n\le(1+o(1))\ln\ln V_n$ on every path with bounded mixture wealth and $V_n\to\infty$, where $V_n$ is an intrinsic variance process. It also attains the optimal asymptotic wealth growth rate under iid alternatives. Under the conditional-mean claim and almost-sure divergence of $V_n$, the sharper regret bound holds almost surely, and its leading constant $1$ is unimprovable. We also give explicit finite-time, path-wise regret bounds. A simple hedging principle shows how splitting initial wealth between two strategies achieves a best-of-both-worlds guarantee by retaining the smaller of their regrets and the larger of their growth rates. We contrast our results to those for unbounded data in Agrawal and Ramdas (2026). Their worst-case regret is unbounded. However, hedging yields almost-sure iterated-logarithmic regret together with optimal growth. Finally, our wealth process witnesses a sharp game-theoretic upper law of iterated logarithm, analogous to Shafer and Vovk (2005).
item.dc:creator: Shubhada Agrawal, Aaditya Ramdas

item.title: Kernel-based independence and mean independence tests for weakly dependent data
item.description: arXiv:2604.28104v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We provide a unified framework for independence and mean independence tests based on the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, extending some previous results in the literature to hold in general topological spaces. We also present a complete theoretical analysis of the test statistic asymptotic behavior when the observed sample corresponds to a partial sample path of some stationary and ergodic stochastic process under near epoch dependence assumptions. In particular, we explore the test statistic consistency and limit distribution under both fixed and local hypothesis. The finite sample performance of the test(s) is illustrated with a succinct simulation study involving functional data.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Diz-Castro, Manuel Febrero-Bande, Wenceslao Gonz\'alez-Manteiga

item.title: Higher-Order Neyman Orthogonality in Moment-Condition Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.10842v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We construct moment functions that are Neyman-orthogonal to a chosen order in parametric moment condition models involving nuisance parameters. These moment functions reduce sensitivity to estimation error in the nuisance parameters and, as such, offer a unified and tractable route to higher-order debiasing in a wide range of econometric models. The number of additional nuisance parameters required by our construction, beyond those already present in the original moment conditions, is independent of the order of orthogonalization and can be reduced to a single scalar if desired.
item.dc:creator: St\'ephane Bonhomme, Koen Jochmans, Whitney K. Newey, Martin Weidner

item.title: Learning from Totally Unpaired Data via Minimum Conditional Entropy Coupling
item.description: arXiv:2605.16229v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Consider an "unsupervised classification" setting, where the goal is to learn a predictor of the categorical class variable $X$ using the categorical feature variables $Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$, but we can only train the predictor on $m+1$ totally unpaired datasets, where each dataset only consists of unordered samples of one of the variables $X,Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{m}$. Although this problem is highly underdetermined, we demonstrate that, under the assumption that a predictor with small cross entropy loss exists, we can find a good predictor by coupling the marginal distributions of $X,Y_1,\ldots,Y_m$ in a manner that minimizes the conditional entropy $H(X|Y_1,\ldots,Y_m)$. This problem, which we call minimum conditional entropy coupling (MCEC), is a generalization of the widely studied minimum entropy coupling problem (where $m=1$). Although the MCEC problem is NP-hard, we give an algorithm with a time complexity that is polynomial in $N$, which gives a coupling with conditional entropy within $O(\log \log N)$ from the optimum, where $N$ is the dimension of the output coupling. We also evaluate the performance of the MCEC predictor on synthetic and real-world datasets.
item.dc:creator: Cheuk Ting Li, Jun Chen, Shahab Asoodeh

item.title: Estimation and Inference for Win Measures with Multiple Ordinal Endpoints Subject to Missingness
item.description: arXiv:2605.27085v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Win measures, including the win ratio, win odds, net benefit, and desirability of outcome ranking, are increasingly used in randomized clinical trials with multiple hierarchical ordinal endpoints. In practice, however, one or more component endpoints may have missing data. The standard pairwise-comparison approach, which treats pairs with missing outcomes as ties, can produce biased estimates, even if the data are missing completely at random. Although inverse probability of censoring weighting methods have been developed for censored survival endpoints, corresponding methods for addressing missing hierarchical ordinal endpoints are not yet available. To address this gap, we develop inverse probability weighted (IPW) and augmented IPW (AIPW) estimators for win measures with hierarchical ordinal endpoints subject to missing data, allowing missingness to depend on treatment assignment and baseline covariates. The IPW estimator corrects bias by reweighting complete observed outcomes using joint non-missingness probabilities involved in estimating the joint cell probabilities that define the win measures. The AIPW estimator additionally incorporates outcome modeling, potentially improving estimation precision and achieving double robustness. For inference, we derive closed-form variance estimators for both methods based on influence functions. Simulation studies show that the standard approach can be substantially biased, whereas the proposed IPW and AIPW estimators exhibit small bias and near-nominal coverage under their respective identifying and model conditions. Applications to the SCOUT-CAP and ACTT-1 trials illustrate the practical utility of the proposed methods. An R package WinMO is provided for implementation.
item.dc:creator: Yi Liu, Huiman Barnhart, Sean O'Brien, Yuliya Lokhnygina, Roland A. Matsouaka

item.title: Functional Principal Component Analysis for Manifold-Indexed Data
item.description: arXiv:2606.31465v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Functional principal component analysis has traditionally focused on processes indexed by Euclidean domains, although functional observations increasingly arise on curved domains. We develop FPCA for real-valued processes observed with noise at discrete locations on a general Riemannian manifold. We estimate the mean and covariance functions using intrinsic kernel smoothing based on geodesic distance and a normal-coordinate volume correction, with a general weighting scheme accommodating unequal numbers of observations across subjects. We establish $L^2$ and uniform convergence rates for these estimators and derive corresponding error bounds for the estimated eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. These results quantify how manifold dimension, sampling frequency and weighting affect estimation accuracy and characterize the phase transition between sparse and dense sampling regimes. Simulation studies on the circle and sphere, together with real-data applications, illustrate the finite-sample performance of the proposed methodology.
item.dc:creator: Chang Jun Im, Jeong Min Jeon

item.title: Federated multiple testing with quantized p-values under family-wise error control
item.description: arXiv:2609.19708v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Several institutions test one family of hypotheses under family-wise error control but cannot pool their data, so each site releases only a quantized report of its p-value for each hypothesis, such as whether the p-value is significant. The report's resolution is the number of values it can take. We quantify the power lost to such reports relative to the most powerful centralized procedure given all p-values (the oracle), with reports and combining rule chosen optimally. A report from which the p-value can be recovered loses no power, so the loss is due to compression, not decentralization. Under the stated regularity and power-objective conditions, every finite resolution loses power, and the optimal loss decays as the inverse square of the resolution: equal-width intervals attain this order, and no partition into as many cells improves it. In two-site Beta examples, optimized one-bit reports are nearly lossless for a single hypothesis but lose several times as much power for two. At level 0.05 with two Beta(1,2) hypotheses, optimally combined three-bit equal-width reports retain 99.2% of oracle power. We give the power-optimal combining rule for given reports, and a rule using only their exactly known null distribution, valid under arbitrary dependence across hypotheses.
item.dc:creator: Prasanjit Dubey, Xiaoming Huo

item.title: Streaming PCA: averaging from a geometric perspective
item.description: arXiv:2609.23332v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study principal component analysis (PCA) under memory constraints, a setting that is increasingly important in large-scale data analysis. Our focus is on Oja's algorithm, which is a one-pass, memory-efficient algorithm requiring only $O(p)$ storage in the rank-one case and $O(pk)$ storage for $k$- PCA. The main goal is to develop a procedure based on Oja's algorithm that is optimal without prior knowledge of the eigengap, which is otherwise needed to tune the learning rates effectively. We do this by first introducing a geometric perspective on the convergence of $k$-PCA: by embedding the Oja iterates into the exterior space, we establish an exact equivalence between $k$-PCA in the ambient space and $1$-PCA in the exterior space. This geometric viewpoint enables us to establish several convergence guarantees, including one based only on a single learning-rate schedule. Building on this geometric perspective, we develop an averaging theory for $k$-PCA and show that the resulting averaged estimator is adaptive: it achieves the nearly optimal convergence rate without prior knowledge of the eigengap. As an application, we construct memory-efficient estimators for elliptical component analysis (ECA) \cite{han2014scale,han2018eca}. Simulation studies and real data analysis are conducted to demonstrate the benefits of our proposed algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Tuan Pham, Alessandro Rinaldo, Purnamrita Sarkar

item.title: PICPIs: Prediction-Interval-Conditional Prediction Intervals
item.description: arXiv:2609.25388v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A classical question in statistics is which observable quantities to condition on when drawing inferences about unobservable targets. For conformal prediction in nonparametric uncertainty quantification, standard marginal validity offers limited resolution at the prediction values on which decisions are based, and fully conditional guarantees with respect to the covariates are provably unattainable. We address this gap by introducing a prediction-based conditioning framework that we refer to as Prediction-Interval-Conditional Prediction Intervals (PICPIs). Formally, a PICPI is an interval $I$ satisfying a self-consistency condition: $$\mathbb{E} [Y \mid p(X) \in I] \in I,$$ for predictive model $p$, contextual covariate $X$, and outcome $Y$. Thus, an interval simultaneously defines a stratum of prediction values and certifies that the mean outcome in that stratum lies in the same interval. This self-consistency condition yields data-adaptive strata without altering the original prediction. Such intervals can be constructed using practical algorithms. Under regularity of the prediction distribution, the constructed intervals cover all but an arbitrarily small fraction of prediction values and have widths that decrease at rate $n^{-1/3}$, up to logarithmic factors and the prediction error. Moreover, identifying these locally calibrated intervals can, in turn, inform downstream decision-making. We derive inference procedures for PICPIs in probabilistic prediction and multi-class classification, accompanied by theoretical guarantees. Empirical results are provided that compare PICPIs with existing interval-based baselines.
item.dc:creator: Xuelin Yang, Baihe Huang, Yilong Hou, Guido Imbens, Michael I. Jordan

item.title: Sequential resetting procedures and false discovery rate
item.description: arXiv:2610.09339v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Data arrive sequentially, each associated with a null hypothesis. We develop testing procedures to locate intervals in which some null hypotheses fail, with false discovery rate (FDR) control. The new procedures are called sequential resetting procedures, and they are based on e-values and test supermartingales. We also develop a refined version of the procedures by dropping less informative data points before the block minimum of the test supermartingale in each rejection block. These procedures have explicit FDR bounds under two settings: a classic setting of independence and the more general setting of possible dependence across null data and non-null data. These FDR bounds are independent of the testing horizon, and the general one has anytime validity, but it has an extra logarithm factor compared with the standard FDR level. We present simulation studies and data experiments with applications of sequential resetting procedures to LLM watermark detection and financial backtesting.
item.dc:creator: Qiuqi Wang, Ruodu Wang, Zhenyuan Zhang

item.title: Anchored multiple testing: a transparent use of e-closure to improve FDR procedures
item.description: arXiv:2610.11279v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The recent e-closure method can recover every procedure that controls FDR (and other expectation losses). But the recovered e-collection is ``self-referential'' and gives no insight on how to improve the procedure (if improvable), and some recent improvements have been somewhat opaque. We introduce an elementary new technique called anchoring that exploits looseness in existing FDR proofs to enlarge a baseline multiple-testing procedure's self-referential local e-value. The resulting e-closure thus transparently retains every baseline discovery (and usually adding more) and controlling the false discovery rate under the same conditions as the baseline. To show that this principle is broadly applicable, we use it to improve a large suite of multiple testing procedures: (i) Anchored-BH dominates the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure under PRDS while being incomparable to Goeman's recent closed-BH, (ii) Anchored-BY dominates the Benjamini-Yekutieli (BY) procedure under arbitrary dependence while being incomparable to closed-BY, (iii) For two-sided Gaussian p-values (under appropriate covariance conditions), Anchored-2BH dominates running BH twice at half the level on two one-sided p-values, (iv) Anchored-dBH dominates dependence-adjusted BH, (v) Anchored e-BH dominates e-BH and is incomparable to closed e-BH, (vi) Anchored SeqStep+ improves the original (including selective and adpative variants) while preserving ordered rejection structures. All of these are accomplished in sorting or quadratic time. The appendix shows how to dominate Shifted-BH (for two-sided arbitrarily correlated Gaussians) and NDBH (for negatively dependent p-values), IndBH (for graph-dependent p-values), some online FDR procedures and the support line procedure for boundary FDR control.
item.dc:creator: Aaditya Ramdas
